artiest/taana-gardner.text:
Taana Gardner is an American disco and post-disco singer from Newark, New Jersey, born in 1960. Her grandmother was an opera singer and gave her singing lessons from the age of five. By eleven she was active in the theatre, and before she was a teenager she had already written plays that were staged at Lincoln Center. Her arrival on the dance scene was really a matter of chance. On Thanksgiving Day 1978 the producer Kenton Nix was looking for a singer for his track Work That Body because the singer he had planned to use had fallen ill. Gardner stepped in and recorded the vocals.

The DJ Larry Levan of the Paradise Garage remixed the track, and it became an instant club hit. So began a run of records for West End Records, a New York label that released a great deal of influential disco. Her debut album Taana Gardner appeared in 1979. In 1981 came Heartbeat, her biggest record. It is a long, tight dance record with a low, slow groove, far removed from the glossy disco of the late 1970s.

Heartbeat continued to resonate for a long time. It served as the basis for other tracks, including in hip hop and in Ini Kamoze's 1995 hit Here Comes the Hotstepper. In this way Gardner is one of the voices that bridge disco, New York club culture and hip hop.
artiest/taana-gardner.listen: Listen to Heartbeat and notice the bass and the drum groove, which keep repeating the same pattern. See if you can hear why a later hip hop producer would want to reuse exactly this piece.

artiest/tadd-dameron.text:
Tadd Dameron, born in 1917 in Cleveland, Ohio, was a jazz pianist, composer and arranger. He had piano lessons from the age of four and taught himself orchestration. He wrote his first arrangements in 1938 for a big band from his home town. In 1940 and 1941 he played piano and arranged for Harlan Leonard and his Rockets in Kansas City. In New York he met Charlie Parker and the young bop musicians.

Dameron is regarded as the most influential arranger of the bop era. He wrote for, among others, Count Basie, Artie Shaw, Dizzy Gillespie, Billy Eckstine and Sarah Vaughan. For Vaughan he wrote If You Could See Me Now together with the lyricist Carl Sigman. In 1948 Gillespie played his large orchestral work Soulphony in Three Hearts at Carnegie Hall, and in 1949 Dameron appeared at the Paris jazz festival with Miles Davis. His own groups of the late 1940s and early 1950s included musicians such as Fats Navarro, Dexter Gordon, Sonny Rollins and Clifford Brown. In 1956 he recorded Fontainebleau and Mating Call, the latter with John Coltrane.

His best-known pieces are Hot House, Our Delight, Good Bait and Lady Bird. Those melodies became standard repertoire. Hot House is written over the chords of What Is This Thing Called Love, a habit in bop: a new melody over an existing chord sequence. Dameron was no great virtuoso, but he wrote melodies and ballads full of atmosphere. Drug problems and illness limited his later work, and he died in 1965.
artiest/tadd-dameron.listen: Listen to Hot House, for instance in a performance by a bop quintet. Notice how the melody follows a line of its own while the chords beneath it are those of What Is This Thing Called Love.

artiest/take-that.text:
Take That is an English pop group from Manchester, put together in 1990 by the manager Nigel Martin-Smith. He wanted a British counterpart to the American boy band New Kids on the Block and built the group around the young songwriter and singer Gary Barlow. Howard Donald, Jason Orange, Mark Owen and the sixteen-year-old Robbie Williams joined through auditions. Barlow sang lead and wrote the songs, Owen and Williams sang along, and Donald and Orange were mainly dancers. In the beginning they performed in clubs, at schools and in gay bars.

The breakthrough came in 1992 with covers of It Only Takes a Minute by Tavares and Could It Be Magic by Barry Manilow, and the debut album Take That & Party. Everything Changes (1993) revolved around Barlow's own songs, with the hits Pray, Relight My Fire and Babe. The high point was Back for Good (1995), from the album Nobody Else, which reached number 1 in many countries and was also a hit in America. Williams left in 1995, and in 1996 the group broke up. In 2006 came a comeback as a foursome with Beautiful World, and in 2010 Williams returned for Progress.

Take That combined the tight dancing and teenage audience of a boy band with songs that one of the group members wrote himself. That was unusual: Elton John pointed out that Barlow set the group apart from other boy bands. Above all Barlow's ballads, carried by strings and harmony vocals, also made the group popular with adult listeners.
artiest/take-that.listen: Listen to Back for Good and notice how the song builds slowly: it begins subdued, and gradually the strings and the harmonies come in. Hear how the chorus sounds fuller with every repetition.

artiest/takeo-moriyama.text:
Takeo Moriyama is a Japanese jazz drummer, born in 1945 in Katsunuma, in Yamanashi Prefecture. As a child he played piano, and only in his late teens did he switch to drums. He studied percussion at the Tokyo University of the Arts. In 1967 he joined the small group of the pianist Yosuke Yamashita, with whom he made various international tours until 1975. That trio, and later quartet, was regarded in Japan as one of the most important free jazz groups.

In 1975 two records appeared: Full Load, with his Percussion Ensemble, and Distant Thunder, released on Enja, with Manfred Schoof, Akira Sakata and Yamashita. In 1977 he moved to Nagoya and began leading his own groups. This produced Hush-a-bye (1978), East Plants (1983), Green River (1984) and Live at Lovely (1991). Besides Yamashita, he played or recorded with Aki Takase, Masahiko Satoh, Peter Brötzmann and Manfred Schoof.

Moriyama is known for his powerful, energetic playing, in which the drums take on a role of their own rather than merely keeping time. He shows that Japanese jazz in the 1970s was in contact with the European and American avant-garde and contributed to it in its own right.
artiest/takeo-moriyama.listen: Listen to Distant Thunder and notice how the drums do not merely keep the beat but drive the saxophone and piano forward with quick, rough strokes.

artiest/talk-talk.text:
Talk Talk was an English band, formed in 1981 by the singer and songwriter Mark Hollis, the drummer Lee Harris, the bassist Paul Webb and the keyboard player Simon Brenner. They began as a synth-pop group and in their early years were often compared with Duran Duran. They had the same record company, EMI, and the same producer, Colin Thurston, and in 1982 they supported that band on tour. Their first album was called The Party's Over and appeared in 1982, with the singles Talk Talk and Today.

After Brenner's departure the group became a trio, with the producer Tim Friese-Greene as Hollis's regular writing partner. The second album, It's My Life from 1984, made the band known above all in Europe, North America and New Zealand, with the singles It's My Life and Such a Shame. In England success remained modest. The Colour of Spring followed in 1986, with Life's What You Make It and Living in Another World. By then it was already clear that Hollis did not want to stay with the pop formula.

With Spirit of Eden in 1988 Talk Talk chose a completely different path. The music sounded spacious, quiet and unpredictable, influenced by jazz and improvisation, and became a forerunner of what is now called post-rock. The album was a commercial failure but won praise from critics. After a quarrel with EMI and a move to Polydor, the group made one more album in 1991, Laughing Stock, in the same spirit. After that it broke up. Hollis released one more solo album in 1998, disappeared from the music world and died in 2019. The leap from synth-pop to almost silent, acoustic music makes Talk Talk a remarkable example of a band that left its own success behind.
artiest/talk-talk.listen: First listen to It's My Life by Talk Talk, and then to a passage from Spirit of Eden. Notice the difference in tempo, in instruments and in the space between the notes.

artiest/talking-heads.text:
Talking Heads was an American band from New York. David Byrne, Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth met at the art school Rhode Island School of Design. They moved to New York and played their first gig as Talking Heads in June 1975, supporting the Ramones at CBGB. Weymouth learned to play bass guitar for the band. The name came from the world of television: the image of a talking head, all content and no action. In 1977 Jerry Harrison joined on keyboards and guitar.

The debut album Talking Heads: 77 produced the first hit, Psycho Killer. After that the band worked with the producer Brian Eno on More Songs About Buildings and Food (1978), Fear of Music (1979) and Remain in Light (1980). On those records the music moved ever further towards funk and West African rhythms, with Fela Kuti as an important example. Once in a Lifetime became a well-known song, partly thanks to its video. In 1983 came Speaking in Tongues with Burning Down the House, and the tour that followed was captured in the concert film Stop Making Sense by Jonathan Demme. After Little Creatures (1985), True Stories (1986) and Naked (1988), the band split up.

Talking Heads came out of the CBGB punk scene but sounded very different from the Sex Pistols: not furious, but nervous, clever and danceable. The staccato guitars, the tight rhythm section and Byrne's jerky vocals, with abstract lyrics, made the band one of the forerunners of new wave. They connected the art school and the dance floor.
artiest/talking-heads.listen: Listen to Psycho Killer and notice Tina Weymouth's bass line, which carries the whole song. Hear how tense and measured Byrne sings, and how halfway through he switches to French.

artiest/tamarii-tipaerui.text:
Tamarii Tipaerui is a vocal group from Tahiti. Its name appears on a recording of a himene tarava, made in Papeete, the island's capital. A himene is a sung song in the Polynesian choral tradition, and tarava is the name of the Tahitian variant, which is performed by groups of singers. The recording was made by the English composer and explorer David Fanshawe, who recorded and preserved a great deal of the islanders' singing and music in the South Pacific.

The singing of such a himene is polyphonic and unaccompanied. Several voices sing at once, each with a line of its own, so that a broad, rolling sound arises. This has nothing to do with Western choral singing from a book, although the Christian mission in the region did play a part in the development of the himene. It is above all a living tradition of the islands themselves.

Little has been written about this group, and that is really the point. The music of Tamarii Tipaerui reached pop history through other people's recordings. Fanshawe's material was later used by the Australian band Gang of Youths, who in 2022 worked fragments of Tahitian himene tarava into their album Angel in Realtime. In this way an old Tahitian choral tradition now resounds in pop music.
artiest/tamarii-tipaerui.listen: Listen to Himene tarava and notice the voices overlapping one another. Do you hear a voice that rises high above the rest, and how does the group sound as a whole?

artiest/tan-dun.text: Tan Dun (born in 1957 in Hunan) worked in the countryside during the Cultural Revolution and afterwards played in an opera company. He studied at the Central Conservatory in Beijing and later at Columbia University in New York. As a concert composer he experimented with water, paper and stones as instruments. For Wo hu cang long (2000) by Ang Lee he wrote music with the cellist Yo-Yo Ma as soloist, with Chinese percussion and the erhu. He won an Oscar for it. For Ying xiong (2002) by Zhang Yimou he chose the violinist Itzhak Perlman and the Japanese drumming group Kodo. In this way he combined Western soloists with Chinese sounds.
artiest/tan-dun.listen: Notice the long, plaintive solo on cello or violin and the Chinese percussion that sets the rhythm of the fight scenes.

artiest/tan-dun-en-yo-yo-ma.text:
Tan Dun is a Chinese composer who is at home both in Western classical music and in the Chinese tradition. Yo-Yo Ma is a cellist who is known all over the world and likes to collaborate with musicians from other musical cultures. Together they made the music for the film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon from 2000, directed by Ang Lee. Tan Dun wrote the score, and Yo-Yo Ma played the cello solos.

The music of the film is a blend of a Western orchestra, Chinese instruments and the singing, searching sound of the cello. This creates a sound that suits a martial arts film that is also a love story. The Eternal Vow is a piece from that music. The cello carries the melody while the orchestra lays the atmosphere beneath the soloist. The sound is soft and melancholy, even when the film itself becomes spectacular.

The film music proved to work far beyond the cinema. The score won an Oscar for best original score in 2001, and brought the sound of the Chinese tradition to a large Western audience. For the film music part of the course, this is a good example of how a composer and a soloist together build a musical world of their own, without the music remaining subordinate to the images.
artiest/tan-dun-en-yo-yo-ma.listen: Listen to The Eternal Vow and notice the cello. Can you hear how the soloist sings like a voice, and which other instruments complement or answer the melody?

artiest/tanburi-cemil-bey.text:
Tanburi Cemil Bey was an Ottoman virtuoso on the tanbur and a composer. He was born in Istanbul in 1873, although some sources give 1871, and he died there on 28 July 1916. He received his first lessons from Kanuni Ahmet Bey and the violinist Kemani Aleksan. His first instruments were the violin and the kanun. He broke off his schooling to devote himself to music. By the age of twenty every tanbur player in Istanbul knew his name.

Cemil Bey renewed the playing technique of the tanbur with an energetic, agile touch, which made the instrument sound lighter. He also played kemençe, lavta and cello, and he invented the yaylı tanbur, a tanbur played with a bow. He excelled in the taksim, an improvised piece on a makam, the melodic mode of Ottoman classical music. He recorded his taksims and compositions on 78 rpm records. As a result his playing was preserved and could influence many generations of musicians.

His son Mesut Cemil Bey, like him, became a well-known tanbur player. For anyone studying the history of recorded music, Cemil Bey matters because his improvisations can still be heard almost a century later. The sound of a player from Istanbul around 1900 has not been lost in his case.
artiest/tanburi-cemil-bey.listen: Listen to Gülizar Taksim and try to hear how the player builds a melody without a fixed metre or accompaniment. Notice the quick, clear touch of the tanbur and the places where he pauses for a moment before continuing.

artiest/tangerine-dream.text: Tangerine Dream was founded in West Berlin in 1967 by Edgar Froese. The group belonged to German electronic rock, also known as Krautrock. In the 1970s they worked with synthesizers and sequencers, devices that keep repeating short patterns automatically. The director William Friedkin asked them to score Sorcerer (1977), their first Hollywood film. Others followed, including Thief (1981) by Michael Mann and Risky Business (1983), with the track Love on a Real Train. For the American version of Legend (1985), their music replaced Jerry Goldsmith's orchestral score. Their pulsing sequencer patterns became the sound of the 1980s thriller.
artiest/tangerine-dream.listen: Notice the fast, repeated sequencer patterns over which slow chords and melodies drift.

artiest/tansen.text: Tansen was born in Gwalior and was a master of dhrupad, the oldest form of North Indian classical singing. After years at the court of Rewa, Emperor Akbar brought him to his own court in 1562, where he became one of the nine jewels. Ragas such as Miyan ki Todi and Miyan ki Malhar bear his name. According to legend he could summon rain, but little is certain about his life, and his year of birth, around 1500, is approximate.
artiest/tansen.listen: No recordings of Tansen exist. Listen to the dhrupad tradition that he shaped: the Dagar singers begin with a long alap without rhythm, in which the raga is built up note by note.

artiest/tante-leen.text:
Tante Leen, whose real name was Helena Kok-Polder, was a Dutch folk singer from Amsterdam. She was born in 1912, the fifteenth of sixteen children, and grew up in the Jordaan, in poverty. She worked as a cleaner and a shrimp peeler. She did not perform for the first time until she was forty-three. Customers at the café where she worked entered her for a talent contest run by the record company Bovema, which in 1955 was looking for the Best Voice of the Jordaan. She came second, behind Johnny Jordaan. After that she was known as the Nightingale of the Willemsstraat.

Tante Leen often performed with Johnny Jordaan, with the accordionist Jan Schallig as accompanist. Many of the lyrics came from Jaap Valkhoff. Her biggest hit was Oh, Johnny, addressed to Jordaan. He answered with Tante Leen, Tante Leen, ik ga een liedje over je zingen. She dedicated her song Ook kleine kinderen worden groot to her son Freddie. In 1960 she opened a café on the Nieuwendijk with her second husband, where she sang every evening. In 1968 she was asked to take part in the Eurovision Song Contest, but she declined. In 1975 she stopped singing. She was a great fan of Ajax and made records such as Ajax Hup Hup Hup and Ajax is niet dood!, which was a duet with Jordaan. She died in 1992, and in 1994 she was given a statue.

Her music is the levenslied, the Dutch genre of sentimental popular song: simple melodies with accordion, and singing that stays close to ordinary life. Together with Jordaan she is regarded as the voice of the Amsterdam anthem of the 1950s and 1960s.
artiest/tante-leen.listen: Listen to Oh, Johnny and notice how accordion and voice together carry a simple, singalong melody, full of Amsterdam feeling.

artiest/tatsuro-yamashita.text:
Tatsuro Yamashita is a Japanese singer, songwriter and producer, born in 1953. He began in the band Sugar Babe, with Taeko Onuki and Kunio Muramatsu, which released its only album, Songs, in 1975. After the group split up in 1976 he signed with RCA and began a solo career with the album Circus Town. In the same year he made the album Niagara Triangle Vol. 1 with Eiichi Ohtaki and Ginji Ito. The breakthrough came in 1980 with the single Ride on Time, which reached number 3 on the Japanese Oricon chart, after which the album of the same name went to number one.

The album For You and Ride on Time are seen as symbols of city pop, the polished Japanese pop of the early 1980s. His best-known song in Japan is Christmas Eve, which appeared in 1983 on the album Melodies and has returned to the charts every Christmas season since. He worked with his wife Mariya Takeuchi, on Plastic Love among other things, and with the American songwriter Alan O'Day, who wrote English lyrics. In 2011 his album Ray of Hope topped the Oricon chart.

Yamashita is known as a master craftsman of sound: some songs he plays and sings entirely himself, with vocals, guitar, synthesizer and drums. The music is predominantly acoustic, but shows great knowledge of analogue and digital recording technique. Since the city pop revival of the 2010s he has also been called the King of City Pop outside Japan.
artiest/tatsuro-yamashita.listen: Listen to Ride on Time and notice the clear production and the layered backing vocals, which he builds up himself.

artiest/taylor-swift.text:
Taylor Swift is an American singer and songwriter. She was born in Pennsylvania in 1989 and is named after the singer James Taylor. After a documentary about Faith Hill she wanted to become a country singer in Nashville. At eleven she visited record companies with her mother, but everyone turned her down. She therefore started to concentrate on writing and learned to play guitar at twelve. When she was fourteen the family moved to the Nashville area. After a performance at the Bluebird Cafe she signed with the new label Big Machine Records, on condition that she could write all her songs herself.

Her debut Taylor Swift (2006) and Fearless (2008) were country records, but songs such as Teardrops on My Guitar, Love Story and You Belong with Me were also played on pop radio. On Red (2012) she worked for the first time with the Swedish producer Max Martin. With 1989 (2014) she made the move to synth-pop, with hits such as Shake It Off and Blank Space. Others followed, including Reputation (2017), Lover (2019), the subdued folk albums Folklore and Evermore (2020) and Midnights (2022). Her songs are often personal and tell, like a diary, of love, quarrels and growing up.

After a dispute with her old label Big Machine over the rights to her first albums, she re-recorded four of those albums, with the addition Taylor's Version. In this way she got the recordings into her own hands after all. Her Eras Tour (2023 and 2024) became the highest-grossing concert tour ever. Swift shows how a songwriter can keep reinventing herself and also stay in control in business.
artiest/taylor-swift.listen: Listen to Shake It Off from 2014. Notice the tight, dry drums, the horns and the handclaps, and how in the chorus Swift keeps repeating the same short words.

artiest/te-rauparaha.text:
Te Rauparaha was a Māori rangatira, warlord and leader of the iwi Ngāti Toa and Ngāti Raukawa. He was probably born in the 1760s, near Kāwhia or in the Waikato valley, and died in 1849. He was one of the most powerful military leaders of the Musket Wars. When Ngāti Toa was driven out of the area around Kāwhia in 1822, he led a fighting migration to the south. It ended with dominion over the south of the North Island and over Kapiti Island. In 1824 he defeated, at Waiorua, a large coalition that wanted to take the island. Annual expeditions to the South Island followed. Because of his conquests he was called the Napoleon of the South.

Te Rauparaha encouraged whaling stations and traded with the Europeans to obtain guns. He signed the Treaty of Waitangi early on and played a central part in the Wairau Affray, which many see as the first fight of the New Zealand Wars. Shortly before his death he oversaw the building of the Rangiātea church in Ōtaki. He made Ngāti Toa one of the richest and most powerful tribes of New Zealand and permanently changed Māori tribal structures.

He was also a gifted composer of haka. Ka Mate is the best known, above all because sports teams perform it before matches. In this way his musical legacy lives on in the worldwide recognition of the haka.
artiest/te-rauparaha.listen: Listen to Ka Mate, performed as a haka, and notice how voice, rhythm and bursts of breath form a single whole, without any instrument.

artiest/teach-in.text:
Teach-In was a Dutch pop group that was active from 1967 to 1980. The band was founded in Enschede, with Koos Versteeg as its leader. In 1971 only Versteeg and the drummer Rudi Nijhuis remained, and the singer Getty Kaspers and the guitarist Chris De Wolde, among others, joined. The producer and co-composer Eddy Ouwens took care of the sound, at the record company CNR. The first single, Spoke the Lord Creator, an adaptation of a song by Focus, failed to chart in 1972. In 1974 the group had three hits in the Dutch top 15: Fly Away, In the Summernight and Tennessee Town.

In March 1975 Teach-In won the Eurovision Song Contest with Ding-a-dong, written by Will Luikinga and Eddy Ouwens. It was the first winner to have performed first. The song charted in almost every European country and reached number 3 in the Netherlands. In October 1975 Goodbye Love followed. After the departure of Kaspers and others new members arrived, and Upside Down reached second place in 1976. The disco wave brought the band into difficulties in 1978. With Dear John, in which they ask John Travolta to teach them to dance, they nonetheless wrote another hit. Regrets was the last song in 1980, after which the group split up. Later the band briefly got back together.

Teach-In made catchy, singalong Dutch pop with a European character. Its success showed that a Dutch group could win the Eurovision Song Contest.
artiest/teach-in.listen: Listen to Ding-a-dong and notice the repeated sound motifs and the simple, almost childlike chorus that makes the song stick.

artiest/tears-for-fears.text:
Tears for Fears is an English pop group from Bath, formed in 1981 by Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal. The two had known each other since their teens and first played in Graduate, a band with mod influences. Then they discovered the electronic music of Tubeway Army, OMD, Depeche Mode and the Human League. Their name comes from the primal therapy of the American psychologist Arthur Janov, a therapy that became well known because John Lennon was a patient.

The debut album The Hurting appeared in 1983 with the singles Mad World, Change and Pale Shelter. The music sounded dark and personal, with lyrics about fear and childhood trauma, in a synth-pop arrangement. Mad World builds its chorus on two chords that move back and forth without the tension resolving. In 1985 came Songs from the Big Chair, with Shout and Everybody Wants to Rule the World. That album became a worldwide success and took both songs to number one on the American Hot 100. Everybody Wants to Rule the World won a Brit Award for best British single in 1986. In 1989 The Seeds of Love was released, with Sowing the Seeds of Love.

After the 1990 tour Smith and Orzabal parted in acrimony. Orzabal went on making albums under the band name, including Elemental in 1993 and Raoul and the Kings of Spain in 1995. In 2000 they reconciled, and in 2004 Everybody Loves a Happy Ending appeared. In 2022 came The Tipping Point. Tears for Fears showed that synth-pop could also have depth, and remained relevant for decades.
artiest/tears-for-fears.listen: Listen to Mad World by Tears for Fears. Notice the two chords in the chorus that keep moving back and forth, and how cool and yet sad the vocals sound on top of them.

artiest/teatro-alla-scala.text:
The Teatro alla Scala, La Scala for short, is a historic opera house in Milan. It opened on 3 August 1778, with Europa riconosciuta by Antonio Salieri. The theatre came about after the previous building, the Teatro Regio Ducale, burned down in 1776 following a carnival gala. The architect Giuseppe Piermarini designed the new house on the site of the church of Santa Maria della Scala, from which it takes its name. It had about three thousand seats, divided between a stalls area and six tiers of boxes with the loggione above them.

Many of the greatest opera singers from Italy and the rest of the world performed here. The house has its own chorus, ballet and orchestra, and the Filarmonica della Scala. The season opens every year on 7 December, the feast day of Saint Ambrose, patron saint of Milan. There is also a museum and an academy for music, dance and stagecraft. In the loggione sits the most critical audience, the loggionisti, who can applaud singers exuberantly or boo them mercilessly. In 2006 the tenor Roberto Alagna left the stage after being booed during Aida.

La Scala is regarded as one of the most important opera and ballet stages in the world. For pop history it matters as a symbol of the classical theatre sound: the place where the great Italian opera tradition of Verdi and Puccini was performed and where vocal technique, orchestra and sets together form a single sonic picture.
artiest/teatro-alla-scala.listen: Listen to a live recording from La Scala of an opera chorus and notice the hall: the audience audibly reacts, and the acoustics give voices and orchestra a clear, spacious sound.

artiest/ted-curson.text:
Ted Curson was an American jazz trumpeter, born in 1935 in Philadelphia. He became interested in the trumpet after seeing a newspaper seller play a silver trumpet. His father would rather have seen him on alto saxophone, like Louis Jordan, but at ten he got his first trumpet. He studied at the Granoff School of Music and in 1956, on the advice of Miles Davis, moved to New York. There he played and recorded with Cecil Taylor in the late 1950s and early 1960s, and in 1959 and 1960 was a member of Charles Mingus's band, including on the recordings of Pre-Bird and at the Antibes festival.

After that he led his own groups and played with, among others, Max Roach, Lee Konitz, Andrew Hill, Booker Ervin and Archie Shepp. His composition Tears for Dolphy, a tribute to Eric Dolphy, has been used in many films. He was a familiar face in Finland, where from 1966 he appeared every year at the Pori Jazz Festival. In 1976 he returned to North America and formed a septet. He lived for a long time in Montclair, New Jersey, and died there in 2012.

Curson played in a style that bridged bebop and the freer jazz of the 1960s. His playing was clear and melodic, and he was known as a musician who could work with both Mingus and Cecil Taylor.
artiest/ted-curson.listen: Listen to Tears for Dolphy and notice the slow, plaintive melody of the trumpet, which expresses grief without words.

artiest/teddy-hill.text:
Teddy Hill was an American big band leader and saxophonist, born in 1909 in Birmingham, Alabama. He played drums, clarinet and soprano and tenor saxophone. In the 1920s he played in New York with the Whitman Sisters, with George Howe and in the orchestra of Luis Russell. In 1934 he started his own band, which had regular slots on NBC radio and played regularly at the Savoy Ballroom. In the summer of 1937 the orchestra toured England and France. Hill recorded for ARC, Vocalion and Bluebird.

His band was a breeding ground for young musicians, such as Roy Eldridge, Bill Coleman, Frankie Newton and Dizzy Gillespie. In 1940 he gave up the big band and became manager of Minton's Playhouse in Harlem. That club became a centre of bebop, with players such as Thelonious Monk and Kenny Clarke. Hill stayed there until 1969, by which time the club's musical importance had long since vanished, and afterwards ran Baron's Lounge. He died in 1978. His daughter, with the singer Bonnie Davis, became known as Melba Moore.

Hill stands in jazz history above all for what he made possible: a big band where young soloists could stand out, and a club where nightly jam sessions cleared the way to bebop.
artiest/teddy-hill.listen: Listen to a recording of Teddy Hill's orchestra from 1935 to 1937 and notice the tight big band horns and the short solos, in which you can hear young musicians such as Dizzy Gillespie.

artiest/teddy-riley.text:
Teddy Riley is an American producer, musician and singer from Harlem in New York. He was born in 1967 and was already active as a teenager as a producer and keyboard player. In the late 1980s he devised a sound that came to be called new jack swing. In it the hard, sampled beats of hip hop came together with the vocals and harmonies of R&B. For this he worked with a drum machine and synthesizers, and in doing so supplied the blueprint for much Black pop music of that time.

With his group Guy he released the self-titled debut album in 1988. He also produced for other artists, including Bobby Brown, and later worked with Michael Jackson on the album Dangerous from 1991. In the 1990s he founded Blackstreet, a vocal group that in 1996 made the hit No Diggity with Dr. Dre.

Riley showed how close hip hop and R&B could come to one another. What he did in the late 1980s then simply became the standard way of making a pop record: a solid beat under a sung melody, with room for a rapper. For a production like his, the studio is just as important as the stage.
artiest/teddy-riley.listen: Listen to No Diggity by Blackstreet. Notice how the beat stays hard and dry while the vocals lie soft and layered on top of it.

artiest/teddy-scholten.text:
Teddy Scholten, born Dorothea Margaretha van Zwieteren, was a Dutch singer and presenter. She was born in The Hague in 1926 and grew up in Rijswijk, the daughter of an amateur actor. In 1944 she met the singer Henk Scholten, whom she married in 1947. In 1950 she was invited by The Coca-Cola Company to appear in a show in the United States, which made her one of the first Dutch pop artists to perform there. She sang on the radio programme De bonte dinsdagavondtrein and from 1955 to 1960 was a guest star on the AVRO television show De Snip en Snap Revue.

In 1959 she won the Nationaal Songfestival with Een beetje, written by Willy van Hemert and Dick Schallies. With it she represented the Netherlands at the Eurovision Song Contest in Cannes. She won with 21 points from the international juries, the second Dutch victory. She also recorded the song in French, German, Italian and Swedish. In 1961 she had a hit with her husband with Bom-be-die-bom, a translation of Goodness Gracious Me from the film The Millionairess. With Henk she recorded several albums, often of children's songs. In 1965 and 1966 she herself presented the Nationaal Songfestival. She died in 2010.

Her songs are light, neat entertainment music from the time before the beat boom, with orchestral accompaniment and a clear singing voice. For Dutch pop history she is above all the face of the early Eurovision period, when the festival became a television event for the whole family.
artiest/teddy-scholten.listen: Listen to Een beetje and notice the light, playful singing and the rhythm of the sentences, with which a small, cheerful declaration of love is told.

artiest/teddy-wilson.text: The pianist Teddy Wilson, with Earl Hines and Art Tatum as his examples, played the most elegant piano style of swing in the 1930s: light, clear lines with the right hand and a calm left hand. He first worked for Louis Armstrong and Benny Carter. From 1935 he led studio groups for the producer John Hammond with which Billie Holiday made her first great records. In the same year he became a member of the Benny Goodman Trio, with Goodman and the drummer Gene Krupa. In this way he was one of the first Black musicians to play openly in a mixed group for a large white audience. Later he led a big band of his own and taught at the Juilliard School.
artiest/teddy-wilson.listen: Notice the light, neat lines of the piano behind the singer.

artiest/television.text:
Television was an American rock band from New York, formed in 1973 around the singer and guitarist Tom Verlaine and the bassist Richard Hell, two friends who badly wanted to be poets. The guitarist Richard Lloyd and the drummer Billy Ficca completed the line-up, and later Fred Smith replaced Hell as bassist. The group grew into a regular name at CBGB, the club where the New York punk scene of the 1970s came into being. The name is a pun on tell a vision.

The debut album Marquee Moon came out in 1977 and is regarded as one of the most important records of the punk era. The follow-up album Adventure from 1978 sounded softer and more contemplative. After that the band split up. In 1991 it came together again and made the album Television, which appeared in 1992. Verlaine died in January 2023.

The music of Television was clearer and technically stronger than that of most punk bands. Verlaine and Lloyd played interwoven guitar parts without a clear rhythm or lead guitarist, and the group drew on influences from jazz and from 1960s rock. The minimalist music of Steve Reich also played a part. In this way Television became an important example for later punk and alternative rock.
artiest/television.listen: Listen to Marquee Moon and notice the two guitars. Try to hear how they alternate and complement each other and how the guitar solo slowly builds.

artiest/tems.text:
Tems, whose real name is Temilade Openiyi, is a Nigerian singer, songwriter and producer. She was born in Lagos in 1995. Her family moved to the United Kingdom when she was still a baby. Her first name means the crown is mine in Yoruba. She became known in 2020 as a guest singer on Essence by Wizkid, a song that earned a Grammy nomination with a remix featuring Justin Bieber. In the same year she sang on Fountains by Drake and released her first EP, For Broken Ears.

After that she signed with RCA Records and in 2021 released the EP If Orange Was a Place. In 2022 Future used a piece of her song Higher in Wait for U, together with Drake. That song entered at number one on the American Hot 100, something no African artist had ever achieved before. She won a Grammy with it. She also covered No Woman, No Cry for the film Black Panther: Wakanda Forever and co-wrote Lift Me Up by Rihanna. In 2024 her debut album Born in the Wild followed.

Tems's style lies between R&B, afrobeats and soul, with a low, warm voice and a calm groove. She is one of the Nigerian artists who entered international pop in the 2020s. That makes her a good example of how afrobeats reached the global pop world.
artiest/tems.listen: Listen to Essence and notice Tems's voice. Do you hear how she sings almost effortlessly through the rhythmic beat, and how the space between the sounds makes that possible?

artiest/ten-city.text:
Ten City is an American R&B and house group from Chicago. The name comes from the word intensity. The group began in 1987 under the name Ragtyme and consisted of the singer Byron Stingily, the guitarist Herb Lawson and the keyboard player Byron Burke. The producer Marshall Jefferson worked in the background and gave the music the sound of Chicago house. Atlantic Records offered Stingily a contract, but he would only sign if his colleagues could come too. That is how Ten City came about.

The debut album Foundation came out in 1989, with the singles Devotion, Right Back to You and That's the Way Love Is. The last of these became a club hit in America and in the United Kingdom in 1989. The group travelled on money borrowed from Stingily's grandmother for a promotional tour of Europe, and it worked. After that came the albums State of Mind in 1990, No House Big Enough in 1992 and That Was Then, This Is Now in 1994. Stingily later went solo, and in 2021 a new album appeared under the name Ten City, Judgement.

Ten City is regarded as one of the first examples of deep house. The music combines Stingily's soft soul voice with tight drum machines and warm synthesizers. The group also played live, which was still unusual for house at the time. In this way it brought the dance floor and soul singing together.
artiest/ten-city.listen: Listen to That's the Way Love Is and notice how Stingily's vocals keep floating above the tight beat. Do you hear the piano and the synthesizers that complement the rhythm of the drum machine?

artiest/tenore-de-orosei.text:
Tenore de Orosei is a vocal group from the village of Orosei in Sardinia. The group sings in the tradition of the cantu a tenore, a polyphonic folk singing that is characteristic of the island, especially of the Barbagia region. The UNESCO committee recognised that singing style in 2005 as intangible cultural heritage. The Tenore de Orosei is known as one of the best-known groups performing this style.

Four men stand in a tight circle and each has a role of his own. The boche sings the solo and delivers a poem in Sardinian; the mesu boche, the contra and the bassu form the chorus. That chorus sings no words, but sounds such as bim-bam-bom. The bassu sings the same note as the solo voice, the contra a fifth above it. The contra and the bassu use a special throat technique for this, so that a deep, rough sound arises. Each village sings it in its own way, so that you can hear from the sound where a group comes from.

The 1998 recording in the course, Cara Cantu Ser Bella, is made in the style called voce seria. Such singing shows that a four-part choir without instruments can create a sound world of its own, one that lies far from pop and rock but still belongs to the same history of singing.
artiest/tenore-de-orosei.listen: Listen to Cara Cantu Ser Bella and notice the voice that begins alone. Do you hear how the other three singers then come in and lay a deep, humming sound beneath it?

artiest/tenores-di-bitti.text:
Tenores di Bitti is a traditional vocal group from the village of Bitti in Sardinia. The group sings in a polyphonic style that is also described as overtone singing, and which according to tradition is thousands of years old. The tenore of Bitti is regarded as one of the best and most traditional groups on the island. There are several groups in Bitti, and the best known is the Tenore di Bitti Mialinu Pira.

Each singer has a part of his own. The boke is the soloist and carries the melody, the bassu gives the root note, the contra sings the fifth and the mesu oke completes the chord with the note an octave above the fifth. In this way it sounds like a single rough, deep chord with the solo floating above it. The group improvises or recites poems. On their albums Romanzesu in 1993 and Ammentos in 1996 this singing reached a wider audience. On the album S'amore 'e mama, released on Real World, you can also hear ambient sounds from the places in Bitti where the recordings were made, such as churches, streets and cafés.

For pop history the group is important because it brought a centuries-old vocal tradition, by way of a world music record label, to an audience outside Sardinia.
artiest/tenores-di-bitti.listen: Listen to Cantu a Ballu Seriu and notice the division of roles. Try to tell the solo voice apart from the deep, almost humming voices beneath it.

artiest/teo-macero.text:
Teo Macero, whose full name was Attilio Joseph Macero, was an American producer, saxophonist and composer. He was born in 1925 in Glens Falls, New York, and studied at the Juilliard School in New York, where he graduated in composition in 1953. That same year he co-founded Charles Mingus's Jazz Composers Workshop. As a composer he wrote, among other things, in third stream, a blend of jazz and classical music. His first own album, Explorations, appeared in 1954.

In 1957 he joined Columbia Records, where he was a producer for twenty years. He worked with Mingus, Duke Ellington, Thelonious Monk, Dave Brubeck, Count Basie and Tony Bennett, and made Brubeck's Time Out and Mingus Ah Um. His best-known collaboration was the one with Miles Davis. He produced or co-produced most of Davis's Columbia work, including Sketches of Spain. On the electric work, such as In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew from 1970, he took on even more the role of co-creator.

Davis and his band played long jams, and Macero cut and spliced the tape into new pieces. He repeated, swapped and reworked fragments, with techniques that later became commonplace in rock, hip hop and dance. Some critics felt he edited too much, but others called this precisely his great merit. His work shows that a studio does not merely capture what musicians play, but is itself an instrument.
artiest/teo-macero.listen: Listen to Bitches Brew by Miles Davis. Notice how passages of music change abruptly, are repeated or almost dissolve, and bear in mind that this was not all played in one go.

artiest/terence-blanchard.text:
Terence Blanchard is an American jazz trumpeter and composer, born in 1962 in New Orleans. His father was an insurance manager and amateur opera singer. He began piano at five and chose the trumpet at eight. As a child he played in summer camps with Wynton and Branford Marsalis, and he studied with Ellis Marsalis at the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts. While studying at Rutgers University he toured with the Lionel Hampton Orchestra. In 1982, on the recommendation of Wynton Marsalis, he took Marsalis's place in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, where he became musical director.

In 1986 he formed a quintet of his own with Donald Harrison, which influenced young jazz musicians such as Christian McBride, Nicholas Payton and Roy Hargrove. His self-titled solo debut appeared in 1990 on Columbia. After work on Do the Right Thing and Mo' Better Blues he composed the music for Jungle Fever (1991). Since then he has scored most of Spike Lee's films, including Malcolm X, Clockers, 25th Hour, Inside Man, BlacKkKlansman and Da 5 Bloods. For the last two he received Oscar nominations. His opera Fire Shut Up in My Bones was staged at the Metropolitan Opera in 2021 and 2022, the first opera by an African American composer there.

Blanchard plays with a warm, singing tone and connects the jazz tradition of New Orleans with film music and opera. He is also a teacher, among other things as artistic director of the Thelonious Monk Institute, and in 2024 he was named an NEA Jazz Master.
artiest/terence-blanchard.listen: Listen to his music for Malcolm X and notice how the trumpet takes on the role of a singing narrator above an orchestra.

artiest/terius-nash.text:
Terius Nash, known as The-Dream, is an American singer, songwriter and producer, born in 1977 in Rockingham, North Carolina, and raised in Atlanta. He learned trumpet, drums and guitar. When his mother died in 1992, he began writing songs, and that gave him a soft spot for women from which songs about female strength later emerged. In 2001 he met the producer Laney Stewart, who helped him to a publishing deal after his song Everything for B2K. With Laney's brother Tricky Stewart he wrote Me Against the Music for Britney Spears and in 2007 Umbrella for Rihanna, which was nominated for Song of the Year.

After that success he signed with Def Jam for albums of his own: Love/Hate (2007), Love vs. Money (2009), Love King (2010), 1977 (2011) and IV Play (2013). He co-wrote Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) and Partition by Beyoncé, Touch My Body by Mariah Carey, Baby by Justin Bieber, All of the Lights by Kanye West and Savage (Remix) by Megan Thee Stallion. Since I Am... Sasha Fierce he has been credited on every subsequent Beyoncé album. He won eight Grammys.

The-Dream's music is R&B with hip hop beats, driving rhythms and high, flowing vocals. As a writer behind the scenes he gave the pop music of the 2000s and 2010s much of its shape, with choruses that stick immediately.
artiest/terius-nash.listen: Listen to Umbrella by Rihanna and notice the repeated, almost hypnotic hook and the tight drum pattern with which the song builds.

artiest/terry-gibbs.text:
Terry Gibbs, born Julius Gubenko in New York in 1924, is an American vibraphonist and band leader. At twelve he won an amateur contest as a xylophonist. During his military service he played drums in army bands. Afterwards he worked in New York with Bill DeArango and in 1946 recorded with Tiny Kahn in Aaron Sachs's quintet. He played or recorded with Tommy Dorsey, Chubby Jackson, Buddy Rich, Woody Herman, Benny Goodman, Alice Coltrane, Louie Bellson and Mel Tormé. In the 1950s he appeared on American television, including on Steve Allen's programme, with which he played lively vibraphone duets. In 2024 he turned a hundred.

In 1958 he moved from New York to California. There he built a big band of his own, the Dream Band. In 1959 it played in Los Angeles at the clubs Seville and Sundown, on evenings when the best jazz and studio musicians in Hollywood were available. The regular core had Mel Lewis on drums. Important players were Joe Maini, Bill Holman, Med Flory, Al Porcino, Conte Candoli and Frank Rosolino. Arrangements came from, among others, Bill Holman, Marty Paich and Al Cohn, written so that Gibbs's vibraphone was in the foreground. Between 1959 and 1961 four albums appeared, including Swing Is Here! and Explosion!. Later more live tapes were released.

Gibbs plays fast and fiery, with a light, clear vibraphone sound above a swinging big band. His Dream Band is regarded as an example of West Coast big band jazz, and he won Down Beat and Metronome polls.
artiest/terry-gibbs.listen: Listen to a track by the Dream Band from Swing Is Here! and notice how the vibraphone keeps sounding above the swelling horns.

artiest/terry-lewis.text:
Terry Lewis, born in 1956, is one half of Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, an American production and songwriting team in R&B and pop. He met Jimmy Jam, whose real name is James Harris, on a University of Minnesota programme. Lewis was in the band Flyte Tyme, which Harris later joined. In 1981 Prince turned it into the group The Time, and the two played on almost all of their albums.

The duo was thrown out of The Time when a snowstorm in Atlanta prevented them from performing while they were secretly making music for the S.O.S. Band. One of those songs, Just Be Good to Me, became a hit and established their reputation. They founded Flyte Tyme Productions and worked for, among others, Cherrelle, Alexander O'Neal and Change. They were early users of the Roland TR-808 drum machine. Their big breakthrough came with Janet Jackson, with the album Control from 1986, for which they received a Grammy. Rhythm Nation 1814 followed in 1989 and became one of the best-selling albums ever.

In 1991 they started the label Perspective Records, with Sounds of Blackness among others. In 2022 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. What characterises their work is a tight, driving Minneapolis sound, with hard electronic drums, dense synth layers and a cleanly structured pop song on top. That sound became a trademark of the 1980s and 1990s.
artiest/terry-lewis.listen: Listen to When I Think of You by Janet Jackson. Notice how tightly the drums and the synth bass lock together, and how the vocals glide lightly over them.

artiest/terry-riley.text:
Terry Riley is an American composer and performer, born in 1935 in California. He grew up in Redding and studied composition in San Francisco and at the University of California at Berkeley. He worked with La Monte Young, was involved in the San Francisco Tape Music Center, where he met Steve Reich, Pauline Oliveros and others, and played in New York in Young's Theatre of Eternal Music. For a long time he travelled through Europe and played piano in piano bars to make a living.

His best-known work is In C, a composition from 1964 that appeared on record in 1968. It consists of short melodic motifs that each musician repeats at their own pace, so that a continuously shifting whole arises. In 1969 came the album A Rainbow in Curved Air, with keyboard instruments and tape delay. After that he studied with the Indian singer Pandit Pran Nath and later explored just intonation, as in Shri Camel. He often collaborated with the Kronos Quartet and with his son, the guitarist Gyan Riley.

Riley is regarded as a pioneer of minimal music. His work, with repetition, tape delay and improvisation, has influenced experimental music, rock and contemporary electronic music. In C is therefore a good starting point for anyone who wants to hear how minimal patterns were translated into pop music.
artiest/terry-riley.listen: Listen to In C and notice the constantly recurring pulse in the high notes. Do you hear how the whole slowly changes colour while the musicians repeat their motifs?

artiest/terumasa-hino.text: The trumpeter Terumasa Hino was born in Tokyo in 1942. His father was a tap dancer and trumpeter, and Hino began as a child with tap dancing before he took up the trumpet. As a teenager he played in clubs for American soldiers. In the late 1960s he became known in Japan with his quintet; Hi-Nology (1969) was his breakthrough. In 1975 he moved to New York, where he played with, among others, Gil Evans, Elvin Jones and Jackie McLean. He followed the developments of his time, from hard bop and modal jazz to fusion: City Connection (1979) became a big success. His brother Motohiko Hino was a drummer.
artiest/terumasa-hino.listen: Listen to the fierce trumpet above a tight, electric groove.

artiest/tex-beneke.text:
Tex Beneke, whose full name was Gordon Lee Beneke, was an American saxophonist, singer and band leader, born in 1914 in Fort Worth, Texas. He began on saxophone at nine and, after trying soprano and alto, stayed with the tenor. His first professional work was in 1935 with the band leader Ben Young. The drummer Gene Krupa heard the band, wanted to take Beneke with him and recommended him to Glenn Miller, who put a band together in 1938. Miller immediately made him his most important tenor soloist.

Beneke played almost all the tenor solos on the recordings and performances of the Miller orchestra until it was disbanded in 1942. In In the Mood, recorded on 1 August 1939, he trades two-bar solos with his colleague Al Klink. They do so in A String of Pearls (1941) as well. He sang Chattanooga Choo Choo, which in 1942 received the first gold record ever, and I've Got a Gal in Kalamazoo. Beneke appeared in the films Sun Valley Serenade (1941) and Orchestra Wives (1942), which took him high in the Metronome polls. After the band was disbanded he had an orchestra of his own, which is linked to the careers of, among others, Eydie Gormé and Henry Mancini.

Beneke stands for the sound of the swing band of the early 1940s: a warm, round tenor and a relaxed, friendly vocal style. The jazz critic Will Friedwald counts him among the important blues vocalists with the big bands of that period.
artiest/tex-beneke.listen: Listen to In the Mood by the Glenn Miller Orchestra and notice the two-bar tenor solos that Beneke and Al Klink play back and forth like a conversation.

artiest/tex-ritter.text:
Tex Ritter, whose full name was Woodward Maurice Ritter, was an American country singer and actor. He was born in 1905 in Murvaul, Texas, and grew up on his family's farm. He studied at the University of Texas in Austin and later at Northwestern Law School, but eventually chose show business. In 1928 he sang on the radio in Houston, on a programme of mainly cowboy songs. That same year he went to New York, where he stood in a male chorus on Broadway. He played the cowboy in Green Grow the Lilacs, the stage forerunner of the musical Oklahoma!

In 1936 he moved to Los Angeles and made his debut on the silver screen in Song of the Gringo. He appeared in seventy films. His greatest recording career began in 1942, when he became the first artist to sign with the new label Capitol Records. In 1944 he had a national hit with I'm Wastin' My Tears on You. In 1952 he sang the title song of the film High Noon, the Ballad of High Noon, which won an Oscar for best song. He also sang the song himself at the ceremony in 1953.

Ritter is regarded as an early pioneer of country music and is in the Country Music Hall of Fame. His cowboy songs and his role in Westerns made him known to a wide audience. He was the father of the actor John Ritter.
artiest/tex-ritter.listen: Listen to High Noon, Do Not Forsake Me, Oh My Darlin' and notice how the song sums up the story of the film. Try to hear how the voice carries the tension with little accompaniment.

artiest/thad-jones.text:
Thad Jones was an American jazz trumpeter, composer and big band leader. He was born in 1923 in Pontiac, Michigan, into a musical family of ten. His older brother Hank was a pianist and his younger brother Elvin a drummer. Thad taught himself to play and became a professional musician at the age of sixteen. During the Second World War he played in American army bands. Afterwards, in 1954, he became a member of Count Basie's orchestra. For that band he wrote almost two dozen arrangements and compositions, including The Deacon and H.R.H.

In 1963 he left Basie's orchestra and worked as an arranger in New York. With the drummer Mel Lewis he founded the Thad Jones/Mel Lewis Orchestra in 1965, which began in 1966 at the Village Vanguard. He led the band for twelve years. In 1978 it won a Grammy for Live in Munich. Later he moved to Copenhagen, where he led the Danish Radio Big Band and made it one of the best in the world. In 1979 he founded a new big band, Eclipse.

Thad Jones is regarded as one of the greatest trumpet soloists in jazz and also as one of the most important writers for big band. A Child Is Born, which appeared in 1970, is one of his best-known compositions. It shows how he used the large ensemble for a lyrical, quiet melody.
artiest/thad-jones.listen: Listen to A Child Is Born and notice the melody. Do you hear how the soloist and the orchestra take turns without the calm of the piece being lost?

artiest/the-age-of-love.text:
The Age of Love is the name of an Italian-Belgian duo and of their song of the same name, which is regarded as one of the first popular examples of trance. It appeared in 1990 as a single on the Belgian label DiKi Records. The song was written by Bruno Sanchioni and Giuseppe Chierchia and produced by Sanchioni and the label boss Roger Samyn, in the studio in Mouscron in Belgium. Sanchioni was working on an instrumental demo and felt that it needed a sample, preferably sung by a woman.

The spoken English lines Come on, dance with me were recorded by the French dancer Valérie Honoré. For years her name was unknown, and some sites attributed the voice to Karen Mulder. Only in 2021 was she credited on vinyl reissues. In the original versions there is also a rough male rap by Chierchia, which is absent from the remixes.

The best known is the 1992 remix by the German duo Jam and Spoon, subtitled Watch Out for Stella Remix. The song continues to be remixed and to appear on compilations to this day, and the latest remix, by Vini Vici and Dimitri Vegas and Like Mike, came out in 2022. In this way The Age of Love is an example of how a club track with repeating synthesizer lines, a pounding beat and a short female voice keeps reaching new generations.
artiest/the-age-of-love.listen: Listen to the 1992 remix by Jam and Spoon and notice the repeating synthesizer line that keeps climbing higher, and the short female voice that makes itself heard above the beat.
